views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current tariff posture without implementing the $300B tranche, and use the upcoming G20 meeting with Xi as a structured negotiation window. The Huawei entity-list action already demonstrates resolve and creates leverage — pressing further with across-the-board consumer tariffs risks self-inflicted damage that outweighs marginal negotiating gain.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE:

Threat Score (+0.35): The dispute has escalated into a genuinely dangerous phase. The US has already imposed 25% tariffs on ~$250B of Chinese imports and placed Huawei on the Entity List, cutting off a major tech firm from US suppliers (timeline: May 15-16). China has matched with retaliatory tariffs on ~$60B of US goods (May 13) and signaled the 'unreliable entity list' (May 31). The OECD warns full escalation could shave 0.7% off global GDP and 0.8% off US GDP by 2021-22 (OECD, May 21). A $300B tariff tranche — covering consumer electronics, clothing, and appliances — would hit American households directly, adding ~$500/year in costs per family (NPR, May 13). Farmers are already suffering from lost Chinese soybean markets. Meanwhile, China has an asymmetric weapon: rare earth minerals, where the US relies on China for 80% of imports (USGS data, CNBC May 30). Xi's visit to a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi (timeline: May 20) was a deliberate signal. The threat is real but not yet existential — the US economy is still growing, and the tech leverage (Huawei) actually favors Washington.

Action Score (-0.15, negotiate): Several factors counsel restraint rather than further escalation. First, the $300B tranche would be the first to hit consumer goods directly — phones, laptops, clothing — creating visible pain for American households right as the 2020 campaign begins. Second, the Huawei Entity List action has already demonstrated US willingness to use non-tariff tools aggressively, which is a stronger leverage signal than yet more tariffs. Third, China has signaled willingness to continue talks (Liu He after May 10 round), and the G20 in late June provides a natural summit window. Fourth, further escalation risks triggering the rare-earth countermeasure, which would hit US defense and tech supply chains in ways that tariffs cannot easily address. The rational play is to consolidate current leverage (25% tariffs on $250B + Huawei restrictions), freeze the $300B threat as a credible deterrent rather than implementing it, and pursue a structured negotiation at the G20. This is not weakness — it is leveraging maximum pressure without crossing the line where self-inflicted damage erodes US bargaining position.
key_factors: $250B tariffs already in effect at 25%; $300B tranche threatened but not yet implemented
Huawei Entity List action (May 15-16) creates strong tech leverage
China rare-earth threat: US 80% import-dependent, Xi's Jiangxi visit signals intent
OECD warns 0.7% global GDP hit from full escalation, 0.8% US GDP in worst case
Consumer cost impact: ~$500/household/year from current tariffs, much more from $300B tranche
Farm sector under severe pressure from lost Chinese soybean markets
China's 'unreliable entity list' (May 31) signals retaliatory tool expansion
G20 summit provides natural Trump-Xi negotiation window in late June

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump signs Executive Order 13873 (securing information/communications technology supply chains). Commerce moves to restrict Huawei.
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.

Google suspends Huawei's access to Android updates / GMS; major US chip suppliers pause sales. Same day: Xi Jinping visits a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi (widely read as a signal on rare-earth leverage).
China announces it will establish an 'unreliable entity list' targeting foreign firms that cut supplies to Chinese companies for non-commercial reasons.
OECD said an intensification of the dispute would likely knock as much as 0.7% off the level of global GDP by 2021-22. Under the worst-case scenario, US GDP would be more than 0.8% lower.
U.S. consumption of rare earth compounds and metals relies heavily on imports, which rose to $160 million in 2018. Eighty percent were from China.
New tariffs increased consumer costs by $1.4 billion a month. Additional tariffs on remaining $300B would boost prices on a broader number of finished goods.
